doc.title: Wendy Oxenhorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 22, 2026

title: Conceiving Great Night in Harlem and finding funding
summary: Inspired by the Jean Bach documentary she wanted a concert at the Apollo, and Herb Storfer's banker neighbor gave 15 thousand dollars.

blocks.x: coming back and I introduced him, I asked him to do a gig with this young musician and they got tight. And before we knew it young musicians were asking him to sit in at clubs. So he would guest star. So he was making money. They were getting paid more because they had the famous name and they were becoming like family. So this became a little thing that started happening with some of the elders. So many beautiful things. So okay, Great Night in Harlem. I really didn’t know anything about jazz. In fact I could tell you that up until a couple of years ago I mean it’s so embarrassing, but I thought, I’m not even going to say it, but there was a great legend who was a piano player, I mean he was a saxophonist, and I thought he was a piano player. Okay? I thought he played piano, okay? So just there you go. So I wanted to learn about jazz and I watched the Jean Bach documentary, “A Great Day in Harlem.” So I figured I’ll learn about everyone. And I thought to myself wouldn’t it be incredible to get all the living legends together and do a great night in Harlem. And do it in Harlem. So I thought of the Apollo Theater. But it was like fifteen thousand dollars at the time to rent it, and no one had done jazz or blues there in like I think it was 30 or 50 years. So I went back to my board and I told them this great idea and they said, “Wendy, first of all we’re not concert producers. You’re not a concert producer. We can’t do this. Plus we don’t have fifteen thousand dollars.” So I said, “Okay, listen, why don’t we look into getting someone who maybe could do that, who knows how to do that.” So we interviewed one person and she wanted a hundred thousand dollars to do it. So we were like okay let’s do this the Wendy way, okay, like the single parent Wendy way. So I said, “Do we know anyone with money? And Herb Storfer, the original founder who I love, he was the 80-year-old who could no longer help the musicians. He would, by the way, pull money out of his pocket. If someone had a heart attack they’d come to his apartment. That’s how the Jazz Foundation used to run. And he would give them five hundred for their rent. The guy was a saint. And so they said, he said, “I know one rich person” and he said, “my neighbor.” And he loves the little events we have in my apartment.” I said, “Okay, good, what is he?” He goes, “I think he’s a merchant banker.” So I got in touch with the guy the next day. We went to lunch. And I told him what was happening, I told him where we were, the kind of need these great musicians – turned out that he was learning blues guitar on his own, he loved the music, he loved the whole idea, and he goes, “I’ll give the 15 thousand dollars for the rent of the Apollo.” I was like woo-hoo. So we were on our way. Now there was no way I could do this alone, so I think I went to George Wein’s Festival Productions and asked, because George Wein had known of what we were doing. He never thought the idea would go well because he said it’s going to be a bottomless pit. These guys can’t – their medical costs alone would be – nobody would have enough money for that.
